L1: # `os` — Miscellaneous operating system interfaces【0†¶】
L2: 
L3: Source code: 【1†Lib/os.py†github.com】
L4: 
L5: * * *
L6: This module provides a portable way of using operating system dependent functionality. If you just want to read or write a file see 【2†`open()`】, if you want to manipulate paths, see the 【3†`os.path`】 module, and if you want to read all the lines in all the files on the command line see the 【4†`fileinput`】 module. For creating temporary files and directories see the 【5†`tempfile`】 module, and for high-level file and directory handling see the 【6†`shutil`】 module.
L7: Notes on the availability of these functions:
L8: 
L9:   * The design of all built-in operating system dependent modules of Python is such that as long as the same functionality is available, it uses the same interface; for example, the function `os.stat(path)` returns stat information about path in the same format (which happens to have originated with the POSIX interface).
L10:   * Extensions peculiar to a particular operating system are also available through the 【0†`os`】 module, but using them is of course a threat to portability.
L11: 
L12:   * All functions accepting path or file names accept both bytes and string objects, and result in an object of the same type, if a path or file name is returned.
L13: 
L14:   * On VxWorks, os.popen, os.fork, os.execv and os.spawn*p* are not supported.
L15:   * On WebAssembly platforms `wasm32-emscripten` and `wasm32-wasi`, large parts of the 【0†`os`】 module are not available or behave differently. API related to processes (e.g. 【7†`fork()`】, 【8†`execve()`】), signals (e.g. 【9†`kill()`】, 【10†`wait()`】), and resources (e.g. 【11†`nice()`】) are not available. Others like 【12†`getuid()`】 and 【13†`getpid()`】 are emulated or stubs.
L16: 
L17: Note
L18: All functions in this module raise 【14†`OSError`】 (or subclasses thereof) in the case of invalid or inaccessible file names and paths, or other arguments that have the correct type, but are not accepted by the operating system.
L19:

L21: 
L22: 
L23: An alias for the built-in 【14†`OSError`】 exception.

L13:            device

L18:            Standard C library (libc, -lc)

L26: 
L27:        Feature Test Macro Requirements for glibc (see
L28:        【15†feature_test_macros(7)】):
L29: 
L30:            fsync():
L31:                glibc 2.16 and later:
L32:                    No feature test macros need be defined
L33:                glibc up to and including 2.15:
L34:                    _BSD_SOURCE || _XOPEN_SOURCE
L35:                        || /* Since glibc 2.8: */ _POSIX_C_SOURCE >= 200112L
L36: 
L37:            fdatasync():
L38:                _POSIX_C_SOURCE >= 199309L || _XOPEN_SOURCE >= 500
L39: ## DESCRIPTION         【14†top】
L40: 
L41:            fsync() transfers ("flushes") all modified in-core data of (i.e.,
L42:            modified buffer cache pages for) the file referred to by the file
L43:            descriptor fd to the disk device (or other permanent storage
L44:            device) so that all changed information can be retrieved even if
L45:            the system crashes or is rebooted.  This includes writing through
L46:            or flushing a disk cache if present.  The call blocks until the
L47:            device reports that the transfer has completed.
L48: 
L49:            As well as flushing the file data, fsync() also flushes the
L50:            metadata information associated with the file (see 【16†inode(7)】).
L51: 
L52:            Calling fsync() does not necessarily ensure that the entry in the
L53:            directory containing the file has also reached disk.  For that an
L54:            explicit fsync() on a file descriptor for the directory is also
L55:            needed.

L144:                   applied when a new file is created.  If neither O_CREAT nor

L146:                   can thus be specified as 0, or simply omitted).  The mode
L147:                   argument must be supplied if O_CREAT or O_TMPFILE is

L73:        renameat()
L74:            The renameat() system call operates in exactly the same way as
L75:            rename(), except for the differences described here.
L76: 
L77:            If the pathname given in oldpath is relative, then it is
L78:            interpreted relative to the directory referred to by the file
L79:            descriptor olddirfd (rather than relative to the current working
L80:            directory of the calling process, as is done by rename() for a
L81:            relative pathname).
L82: 
L83:            If oldpath is relative and olddirfd is the special value AT_FDCWD,
L84:            then oldpath is interpreted relative to the current working
L85:            directory of the calling process (like rename()).
L86: 
L87:            If oldpath is absolute, then olddirfd is ignored.
L88: 
L89:            The interpretation of newpath is as for oldpath, except that a
L90:            relative pathname is interpreted relative to the directory
L91:            referred to by the file descriptor newdirfd.
L92: 
L93:            See 【17†openat(2)】 for an explanation of the need for renameat().
L94: 
L95:        renameat2()
L96:            renameat2() has an additional flags argument.  A renameat2() call
L97:            with a zero flags argument is equivalent to renameat().
L98: 
L99:            The flags argument is a bit mask consisting of zero or more of the
L100:            following flags:
L101: 
L102:            RENAME_EXCHANGE
L103:                   Atomically exchange oldpath and newpath.  Both pathnames
L104:                   must exist but may be of different types (e.g., one could
L105:                   be a non-empty directory and the other a symbolic link).
L106: 
L107:            RENAME_NOREPLACE
L108:                   Don't overwrite newpath of the rename.  Return an error if
L109:                   newpath already exists.
L110: 
L111:                   RENAME_NOREPLACE can't be employed together with
L112:                   RENAME_EXCHANGE.
L113: 
L114:                   RENAME_NOREPLACE requires support from the underlying
L115:                   filesystem.  Support for various filesystems was added as
L116:                   follows:
L117: 
L118:                   •  ext4 (Linux 3.15);
L119: 
L120:                   •  btrfs, tmpfs, and cifs (Linux 3.17);
L121: 
L122:                   •  xfs (Linux 4.0);
L123: 
L124:                   •  Support for many other filesystems was added in Linux
L125:                      4.9, including ext2, minix, reiserfs, jfs, vfat, and
L126:                      bpf.
L127: 
L128:            RENAME_WHITEOUT (since Linux 3.18)
L129:                   This operation makes sense only for overlay/union
L130:                   filesystem implementations.
L131: 
L132:                   Specifying RENAME_WHITEOUT creates a "whiteout" object at
L133:                   the source of the rename at the same time as performing the
L134:                   rename.  The whole operation is atomic, so that if the
L135:                   rename succeeds then the whiteout will also have been
L136:                   created.
L137: 
L138:                   A "whiteout" is an object that has special meaning in
L139:                   union/overlay filesystem constructs.  In these constructs,
L140:                   multiple layers exist and only the top one is ever
L141:                   modified.  A whiteout on an upper layer will effectively
L142:                   hide a matching file in the lower layer, making it appear
L143:                   as if the file didn't exist.
